data.key_insight: Using a queue allows us to process nodes level by level. By recording the size of the queue at the beginning of each level iteration, we can group all nodes belonging to the exact same level together.

steps.title: Handle Empty Tree
steps.detail: Check if the root is null. If it is, return an empty list immediately.

steps.title: Initialize Queue and Result List
steps.detail: Create a queue (using collections.deque) and push the root node into it. Initialize an empty result list to store the levels.

steps.title: Process Level by Level
steps.detail: While the queue is not empty, determine the number of nodes at the current level using the current length of the queue.

steps.title: Collect Node Values
steps.detail: Iterate through the nodes of the current level, pop them from the queue, append their values to a level-specific list, and push their non-null children into the queue.

steps.title: Store Level Result
steps.detail: Append the completed level list to the main result list and repeat until the queue is empty.

data.reference_solution:
def levelOrder(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> List[List[int]]:
    if not root:
        return []
    
    nodes_with_depth = []
    def dfs(node, depth):
        if not node:
            return
        nodes_with_depth.append((depth, node.val))
        dfs(node.left, depth + 1)
        dfs(node.right, depth + 1)
        
    dfs(root, 0)
    
    max_depth = max(d for d, v in nodes_with_depth) if nodes_with_depth else -1
    result = []
    for d in range(max_depth + 1):
        level_vals = [v for depth, v in nodes_with_depth if depth == d]
        result.append(level_vals)
    return result

data.pattern_summary: Breadth-First Search systematically visits nodes level by level, moving horizontally across the tree before going deeper. Reach for it whenever a problem asks to process or group elements by their distance or depth from the root.

pattern_options.name: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. BFS processes the tree level by level, making it natural to group values by their depth.

pattern_options.name: Depth-First Search (DFS)
pattern_options.feedback: DFS explores as far as possible down each branch first rather than level by level, making grouping by exact depth require extra sorting or filtering steps.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Two pointers is used for linear structures like arrays or strings, not hierarchical tree structures.

pattern_options.name: Greedy
pattern_options.feedback: Greedy makes locally optimal choices at each step for optimization problems, which does not map to traversing all tree nodes level by level.

signals.phrase: Traverse the tree level by level
signals.hint: This explicitly points away from standard depth-first traversal and toward processing nodes grouped by their depth.

data.brute_force_idea: The brute force approach uses a recursive DFS to visit every node while tracking its depth, storing all nodes in a list as tuples of (depth, value). Then, it finds the maximum depth and loops through each possible depth from zero upwards, filtering the stored list to collect values belonging to that specific level.
data.brute_force_why: Visiting all nodes takes O(n) time. However, iterating through all depths and repeatedly filtering the list for each depth takes additional passes, resulting in quadratic time for unbalanced trees.
data.bottleneck: The code repeatedly scans the entire list of nodes to filter by depth for every single level, doing redundant work that scales poorly as the number of nodes grows.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how many times the code searches through the list of nodes.
Notice that for every single level, you iterate over the entire dataset again.
Ask yourself if you can collect nodes into their respective levels during the initial traversal instead of filtering afterward.
data.brute_force_code:
def levelOrder(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> List[List[int]]:
    if not root:
        return []
    
    nodes_with_depth = []
    def dfs(node, depth):
        if not node:
            return
        nodes_with_depth.append((depth, node.val))
        dfs(node.left, depth + 1)
        dfs(node.right, depth + 1)
        
    dfs(root, 0)
    
    max_depth = max(d for d, v in nodes_with_depth) if nodes_with_depth else -1
    result = []
    for d in range(max_depth + 1):
        level_vals = [v for depth, v in nodes_with_depth if depth == d]
        result.append(level_vals)
    return result

data.overview: The algorithm performs a Breadth-First Search (BFS) on a binary tree using a queue. By checking the exact number of nodes present in the queue at the start of each iteration, it groups nodes level by level into separate lists.
data.intuition: Imagine standing in line at a ticket counter. You process everyone currently waiting in the line as a single group, while sending their children to the back of the line to form the next group.

Not capturing the queue size before starting the inner loop, which mixes levels together.
Forgetting to check if left or right children exist before appending them to the queue.

data.insight: The brute force solution collects all nodes via DFS and then repeatedly scans the list to group them by depth, resulting in unnecessary repeated work. The optimized BFS solution uses a queue to process nodes level by level in a single pass, utilizing collections.deque for efficient O(1) pops from the left.

derivation.note: The while loop condition runs once for each of the n nodes plus one final check when the queue is empty.
The inner for loop iterates over the exact size of the current level, running a total of n times across all levels.
Popping from the left of a collections.deque takes constant time.
Each child node is pushed to the queue at most once.

data.time_summary: Lines 9 through 22 dominate execution. Every node is added to the queue and removed from the queue exactly once, resulting in linear time O(n). Measured evidence confirms this scaling.
data.space_summary: The queue and the result list store all n nodes, meaning memory scales linearly with the number of nodes at O(n) space.
data.takeaway: When grouping tree nodes by depth or distance, use a Breadth-First Search (BFS) with a queue rather than DFS followed by filtering.
mistakes: Using a standard Python list as a queue instead of collections.deque, which turns pops into O(n) operations and degrades performance.
Forgetting to capture level_size before entering the inner loop, which mixes nodes from different levels together.
Failing to handle the edge case where the root is None, leading to attribute errors.
